newsitem.title: USA: U.S. voices concerns over democracy in Slovakia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. voices concerns over democracy in Slovakia.

text.p: The United States on Thursday expressed concerns about Slovakia's commitment to democracy -- a key consideration in admitting the former communist country to NATO.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the concerns had been made clear to Slovak Foreign Minister Pavol Hamzik, who held talks in Washington this week with Secretary of State Warren Christopher and Defence Secretary William Perry.

Burns said the U.S. concerns related to Slovakia's treatment of minorities. About 600,000 ethnic Hungarians live in Slovakia and their status was an issue in a 1995 basic relations treaty between Slovakia and Hungary.
"The United States has been concerned during the summer months about indications that the government of Slovakia's commitment to democracy has been weakening," Burns told a news briefing.
"The government of Slovakia continues to assure us that it is committed to strengthening democracy. We'd like to see that translated to solid action on the ground."

Burns admitted Slovakia had made "substantial progress" in the last three years towards entering Western systems and had been faced with major challenges in overcoming its communist past, including severe economic problems. "We applaud many of the positive steps that have been taken," he said.
Burns said Hamzik had raised Slovakia's interest in NATO membership, which is also being sought by most other East European states, but U.S. officials had made no promises.

Unlike its neighbour the Czech Republic, whose Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus also visited Washington this week, Slovakia is not considered likely to be in the first wave of former Warsaw Pact countries admitted to NATO.

NATO will hold a summit next year to announce the first countries to be admitted to the Western alliance. As well as the Czech Republic, they are expected to include Poland, Hungary and possibly Slovenia.
